concepts.label: What a Chemical Reaction Is and How We Know One Has Happened
concepts.cardText: In everyday situations such as milk left at room temperature in summer, an iron tawa or nail left in humid air, grapes getting fermented, food being cooked or digested and respiration, the nature and identity of the initial substance have somewhat changed. Whenever a chemical change occurs, a chemical reaction has taken place. When a magnesium ribbon is burnt it burns with a dazzling white flame and changes into a white powder, magnesium oxide, formed by the reaction between magnesium and the oxygen in the air. From the activities with magnesium, lead nitrate with potassium iodide, and zinc with dilute acid, any of these observations helps us decide whether a chemical reaction has taken place: a change in state, a change in colour, evolution of a gas, or a change in temperature.

concepts.topicTitle: Chemical Equations and Conservation of Mass
concepts.label: Word-Equations, Formulae and Skeletal Equations
concepts.cardText: The burning of magnesium in oxygen can be written shorter as a word-equation: magnesium + oxygen gives magnesium oxide. The substances that undergo chemical change, magnesium and oxygen, are the reactants and the new substance formed, magnesium oxide, is the product. The reactants are written on the left-hand side with a plus sign between them and the products on the right-hand side, and the arrowhead points towards the products and shows the direction of the reaction. Chemical equations become more concise and useful when chemical formulae are used instead of words, as in Mg + O2 gives MgO. Such an equation that is not yet balanced is a skeletal chemical equation for a reaction.

concepts.topicTitle: Chemical Equations and Conservation of Mass
concepts.label: Balanced Chemical Equations and the Law of Conservation of Mass
concepts.cardText: By the law of conservation of mass, mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. The total mass of the elements in the products has to equal the total mass of the elements in the reactants, so the number of atoms of each element remains the same before and after a reaction. Hence a skeletal chemical equation has to be balanced. An equation is balanced when the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides of the arrow. To balance, draw boxes around each formula and do not change anything inside them, list the atoms of each element, and start with the compound that contains the maximum number of atoms. Only coefficients are changed, never the formulae, so 4 H2O is used and not H2O4. Balancing Fe + H2O giving Fe3O4 + H2 gives 3Fe + 4H2O giving Fe3O4 + 4H2. This is called the hit-and-trial method, using the smallest whole number coefficient.

concepts.label: Physical States and Reaction Conditions in an Equation
concepts.cardText: A balanced equation does not by itself tell the physical state of each reactant and product. To make it more informative, the physical states are written with the formulae: the gaseous, liquid, aqueous and solid states are shown by (g), (l), (aq) and (s). Aqueous is written when the reactant or product is present as a solution in water. In 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) giving Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g), the symbol (g) with H2O shows that water is used in the form of steam. Usually physical states are not included unless it is necessary to specify them. Sometimes reaction conditions such as temperature, pressure or a catalyst are indicated above and/or below the arrow.

concepts.label: Combination Reactions
concepts.cardText: When calcium oxide, quick lime, reacts vigorously with water it produces slaked lime, calcium hydroxide, releasing a large amount of heat. Calcium oxide and water combine to form a single product, calcium hydroxide. A reaction in which a single product is formed from two or more reactants is known as a combination reaction. A solution of slaked lime is used for whitewashing walls. Calcium hydroxide reacts slowly with the carbon dioxide in air to form a thin layer of calcium carbonate on the walls, formed after two to three days of whitewashing, which gives a shiny finish. Other examples are the burning of coal, C + O2 giving CO2, and the formation of water from hydrogen and oxygen. When two or more substances, elements or compounds, combine to form a single product, the reactions are called combination reactions.

concepts.label: Exothermic Reactions
concepts.cardText: In the reaction of quick lime with water a large amount of heat is evolved and the reaction mixture becomes warm. Reactions in which heat is released along with the formation of products are called exothermic chemical reactions. Other examples are the burning of natural gas, respiration and the decomposition of vegetable matter into compost. We get energy from the food we eat. During digestion, food such as rice, potatoes and bread, which contain carbohydrates, is broken down into simpler substances; the carbohydrates form glucose. This glucose combines with oxygen in the cells of our body and provides energy. The special name of this reaction is respiration, and respiration is an exothermic process.

concepts.label: Decomposition and Thermal Decomposition
concepts.cardText: When ferrous sulphate crystals are heated their green colour changes and the odour of burning sulphur can be smelt. In this reaction a single reactant breaks down to give simpler products: ferric oxide, sulphur dioxide and sulphur trioxide. This is a decomposition reaction. Decomposition reactions are opposite to combination reactions: a single substance decomposes to give two or more substances. Decomposition of calcium carbonate, limestone, to calcium oxide, quick lime, and carbon dioxide on heating is an important decomposition reaction used in various industries; quick lime is used in the manufacture of cement. When a decomposition reaction is carried out by heating, it is called thermal decomposition. Heating lead nitrate gives brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide.

concepts.label: Displacement Reactions
concepts.cardText: When iron nails are dipped in copper sulphate solution for about 20 minutes, the iron nails become brownish in colour and the blue colour of the copper sulphate solution fades. In this reaction iron has displaced or removed another element, copper, from copper sulphate solution. This reaction is known as a displacement reaction. Other examples are zinc with copper sulphate giving zinc sulphate and copper, and lead with copper chloride giving lead chloride and copper. Zinc and lead are more reactive elements than copper, so they displace copper from its compounds. When an element displaces another element from its compound, a displacement reaction occurs.

concepts.label: Double Displacement and Precipitation Reactions
concepts.cardText: When sodium sulphate solution and barium chloride solution are mixed, a white substance that is insoluble in water is formed. This insoluble substance is known as a precipitate, and any reaction that produces a precipitate can be called a precipitation reaction. The white precipitate of barium sulphate is formed by the reaction of sulphate ions and barium ions, and the other product, sodium chloride, remains in the solution. Such reactions in which there is an exchange of ions between the reactants are called double displacement reactions. Two different atoms or groups of atoms (ions) are exchanged in double displacement reactions, and precipitation reactions produce insoluble salts. Mixing lead nitrate and potassium iodide is another case.

concepts.label: Oxidation and Reduction
concepts.cardText: When copper powder is heated in a china dish its surface becomes coated with black copper(II) oxide, because oxygen is added to copper. If hydrogen gas is passed over this heated material the black coating turns brown as the reverse reaction takes place and copper is obtained. If a substance gains oxygen during a reaction, it is said to be oxidised, and if it loses oxygen it is reduced. Here copper(II) oxide loses oxygen and is reduced, and hydrogen gains oxygen and is oxidised. One reactant gets oxidised while the other gets reduced, so such reactions are called oxidation-reduction or redox reactions. A substance that gains oxygen or loses hydrogen is oxidised; one that loses oxygen or gains hydrogen is reduced.

concepts.topicTitle: Everyday Effects of Oxidation: Corrosion and Rancidity
concepts.label: Corrosion
concepts.cardText: Iron articles are shiny when new but get coated with a reddish brown powder when left for some time. This is commonly known as rusting of iron. When a metal is attacked by substances around it such as moisture and acids, it is said to corrode, and this process is called corrosion. The black coating on silver and the green coating on copper are other examples of corrosion. Corrosion causes damage to car bodies, bridges, iron railings, ships and all objects made of metals, specially those of iron, and every year an enormous amount of money is spent to replace damaged iron. Applying paint on iron articles protects them.

concepts.topicTitle: Everyday Effects of Oxidation: Corrosion and Rancidity
concepts.label: Rancidity
concepts.cardText: Fat or oil containing food materials left for a long time change in smell and taste. When fats and oils are oxidised, they become rancid and their smell and taste change. Usually substances which prevent oxidation, called antioxidants, are added to foods containing fats and oil. Keeping food in air tight containers helps to slow down oxidation. Chips manufacturers usually flush bags of chips with a gas such as nitrogen to prevent the chips from getting oxidised.
